title: Acts 26:19–32
context: Paul says he was not disobedient to the heavenly vision but preached in Damascus, Jerusalem, Judea, and to the Gentiles that they should repent, turn to God, and do works worthy of repentance. For this he was seized, but with God’s help he stands testifying only what the prophets and Moses said: that the Christ would suffer, rise first from the dead, and proclaim light to Jews and Gentiles. Festus shouts that Paul is out of his mind, but Paul appeals to Agrippa, who asks whether Paul hopes to make him a Christian so quickly. Paul answers that he prays all his hearers would become as he is, except for the chains. The officials agree Paul could have been released had he not appealed to Caesar.

verses.text: “Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision,
verses.arminianNotes: “So, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.” Paul presents his ministry as simple obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Both traditions see here the right response to God’s call. Reformed writers add that the vision itself produced the obedience it required.

verses.text: but declared first to them of Damascus, at Jerusalem, and throughout all the country of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance.
verses.arminianNotes: He preached first in Damascus, then Jerusalem, throughout Judea, and to the Gentiles, that they should repent, turn to God, and perform deeds worthy of their repentance. The order follows the outline of 1:8.
verses.reformedNotes: Repentance and works are linked as root and fruit. Reformed theology insists the deeds demonstrate repentance rather than earn forgiveness, a point Arminian theology also affirms.

verses.text: For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.
verses.arminianNotes: For this reason the Jews seized him in the temple and tried to kill him.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul names the real cause of the riot: his message to the Gentiles, not any temple crime.

verses.text: Having therefore obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would happen,
verses.arminianNotes: With God’s help he stands to this day, testifying to small and great, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul attributes his survival to God’s help, the fulfillment of the promise in verse 17.

verses.text: how the Christ must suffer, and how, by the resurrection of the dead, he would be first to proclaim light both to these people and to the Gentiles.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Christ must suffer, and by rising first from the dead he would proclaim light both to the people and to the Gentiles.
verses.reformedNotes: Christ is “first” to rise, the firstfruits of the resurrection Paul describes in 1 Corinthians 15:20. Light to the Gentiles echoes Isaiah 49:6.

verses.text: As he thus made his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are crazy! Your great learning is driving you insane!”
verses.arminianNotes: Festus interrupts loudly: “Paul, you are out of your mind! Your great learning is driving you mad.” To a Roman, resurrection sounded like lunacy.
verses.reformedNotes: The outburst illustrates Paul’s own words that the cross is foolishness to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23).

verses.text: But he said, “I am not crazy, most excellent Festus, but boldly declare words of truth and reasonableness.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul answers that he is not mad, “most excellent Festus,” but speaks words of truth and soberness.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul refuses the dichotomy between faith and reason. The gospel is sober truth about public events.

verses.text: For the king knows of these things, to whom also I speak freely. For I am persuaded that none of these things is hidden from him, for this has not been done in a corner.
verses.arminianNotes: The king knows about these things, and Paul speaks freely to him, confident that none of this has escaped his notice, “for this has not been done in a corner.”
verses.reformedNotes: The Christian claim concerns events done in public view, open to investigation by anyone who cares to look.

verses.text: King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
verses.arminianNotes: “King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.” Paul presses for a personal response.
verses.reformedNotes: The question traps Agrippa: denying the prophets would offend his Jewish subjects, but affirming them leads straight to Paul’s conclusion.

verses.text: Agrippa said to Paul, “With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?”
verses.arminianNotes: Agrippa replies, “With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?” His words may be sarcastic, evasive, or half-serious. Arminian preachers have long used the verse to warn against coming close to faith and stopping short.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed preachers make a parallel point: intellectual conviction falls short of saving faith without the Spirit’s inward work. Agrippa feels the force of the argument and still deflects it.

verses.text: Paul said, “I pray to God, that whether with little or with much, not only you, but also all that hear me today, might become such as I am, except for these bonds.”
verses.arminianNotes: Paul answers that he prays to God that, with little or much, not only Agrippa but all who hear him today would become as he is, except for these chains. Arminian readers find here the evangelist’s desire for every hearer’s salvation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Paul prays to God for their conversion, recognizing that only God can bring it about, and still pleads with all.

verses.text: The king rose up with the governor and Bernice, and those who sat with them.
verses.arminianNotes: The king rises, and with him the governor, Bernice, and those seated with them.
verses.reformedNotes: The hearing ends at the king’s initiative. The gospel has been laid before the highest audience Paul has faced so far.

verses.text: When they had withdrawn, they spoke to one another, saying, “This man does nothing worthy of death or of bonds.”
verses.arminianNotes: As they leave, they agree that Paul is doing nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.
verses.reformedNotes: Another official verdict of innocence, now including a Jewish king.

verses.text: Agrippa said to Festus, “This man might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
verses.arminianNotes: Agrippa says to Festus that the man could have been released had he not appealed to Caesar.
verses.reformedNotes: Humanly, the appeal now seems to have trapped Paul. In Luke’s story it is the very means by which God keeps his promise to bring Paul to Rome.
